query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled trace amount of boron (~0.3–0.5 at%) into the equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy will trigger the formation of nanoscale, boron‐induced secondary precipitates uniformly dispersed within a continuous disordered BCC matrix. This microstructural modification will act to blunt crack propagation and enhance dislocation mobility at room temperature, thereby substantially improving ductility without compromising the alloy’s high-temperature yield strength (observed at 1600 °C) or its irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW with a single-phase BCC structure exhibiting excellent high-temperature strength but very poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Minor doping with approximately 0.3–0.5 atomic percent boron (B) during alloy processing to achieve a homogeneous distribution.
generation.conditions: The alloy should be processed under similar thermal histories as the baseline (e.g., high-temperature homogenization and controlled cooling) to allow the boron to promote nanoscale precipitate formation without forming extended brittle intermetallics. Testing conditions include room-temperature mechanical tests, high-temperature (1600 °C) yield assessments, and ion irradiation experiments (e.g., up to ~8 dpa).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent, nanoscale boron-induced precipitates (or grain boundary segregations) within the disordered BCC matrix, which enhance intergranular cohesion and impede crack initiation and propagation.
generation.mechanism: Trace boron doping alters local defect energies and stabilizes a microstructure in which discrete, boron-rich precipitates form at grain boundaries and within grains. These precipitates act to deflect propagating cracks and promote more uniform dislocation motion (and possibly activate limited twinning mechanisms), thereby enhancing ductility at room temperature. At high temperature and under irradiation, the nanoscale precipitates are expected to remain coherent and not act as preferential sites for damage accumulation, thus preserving the alloy’s high-temperature strength and radiation tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to undoped NbMoTaW, the boron-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit a significant increase in room-temperature ductility (e.g., from approximately 4–5% compressive strain to potentially above 15–20% plastic strain) while retaining similar yield strengths at 1600 °C and showing minimal additional irradiation-induced hardening or defect clustering.
generation.baseline: Undoped, equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy with a monophase BCC structure characterized by excellent high-temperature performance and theoretically predicted irradiation resistance but inherently poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The improved properties are expected only if the boron content remains within a low concentration window (∼0.3–0.5 at%) and if the processing avoids the formation of extended brittle phases. Excessive doping might lead to coarse intermetallic compounds that could undermine both ductility and irradiation performance.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings from tungsten-based refractory HEAs where trace B or C doping improved room-temperature ductility while maintaining high-temperature strength (e.g., PMC9586648::web::002::introduction and PMC6397024::web::017::conclusions) and from studies showing interstitial modifications can activate ductile deformation mechanisms (PMC5227964::web::011::deformation_mechanisms). It is uncertain how the unique defect and irradiation dynamics in purely equiatomic NbMoTaW (with predicted irradiation resistance from first-principles) will respond to boron doping, and whether the nanoscale precipitates will remain stable under the extreme conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) baseline equiatomic NbMoTaW and (2) NbMoTaW doped with 0.3–0.5 at% boron using identical processing conditions. Characterize their microstructure using TEM and APT to confirm the formation and distribution of nanoscale boron-rich precipitates. Conduct mechanical tests at room temperature (tension/compression) and at 1600 °C to measure yield strength and ductility. Additionally, perform controlled ion irradiation (e.g., up to 8 dpa or using 3 MeV Fe ions) followed by nanoindentation and TEM examination to assess any variations in irradiation-induced defect formation.
measurements: Room-temperature plastic strain and fracture strain (ductility) from mechanical tests.
Microstructural analysis via TEM/APT to quantify precipitate size, distribution, and phase coherence.
Post-irradiation hardness and defect structure analysis (TEM, XRD).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped NbMoTaW samples do not show a statistically significant increase in room-temperature ductility (e.g., less than a twofold improvement over the baseline) or if the high-temperature yield strength or irradiation resistance is degraded (e.g., exhibiting excessive irradiation-induced defect clustering or a notable drop in yield strength), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) consisting of multiple principle elements provide an avenue for realizing exceptional mechanical, physical and chemical properties. We report a novel strategy for designing a new class of HEAs incorporating the additional interstitial element carbon. This results in joint activation of twinning- and transformation-induced plasticity (TWIP and TRIP) by tuning the matrix phase’s instability in a metastable TRIP-assisted dual-phase HEA. Besides TWIP and TRIP, such alloys benefit from massive substitutional and interstitial solid solution strengthening as well as from the composite effect associated with its dual-phase structure. Nanosize particle formation and grain size reduction are also utilized. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEA thus unifies all metallic strengthening mechanisms in one material, leading to twice the tensile strength compared to a single-phase HEA with similar composition, yet, at identical ductility.

The improved mechanical properties (Fig. 3) and the associated multiple deformation mechanisms (Fig. 4) confirm the success of the new design approach, and its potential economic viability since interstitial alloying elements are much cheaper compared to substitutional alloying elements. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEAs unify all known metallurgical strengthening effects in one single bulk material: i) massive substitutional solid solution strengthening due to multiple principle elements (i.e., Fe, Mn, Co and Cr); ii) interstitial solid solution strengthening by carbon; iii) micro-composite effect from dual-phase structure; iv) nano-particle strengthening from nano-carbides (Figs 2b and 4c); v) nano-twinning induced plasticity effect (TWIP) (Fig. 4b); vi) displacive transformation induced plasticity effect (TRIP) (Fig. 4a); vii) formation of stacking faults (Fig. 4b); viii) grain size reduction (increased grain boundary density); and dislocation hardening (Fig. 4b).

The present work shows the development of a new class of a refractory HEA based on four elements: 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V in atomic percentages measured by both EDS and APT. Samples were grown using a magnetron sputtering deposition system from pure metal targets and characterized before and after irradiation. Microstructures present a single-phase BCC crystalline structure. The films show a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with sizes in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm). Concurrent TEM and APT analyses demonstrate the existence of a second phase rich in Cr and V, first forming lamella-like regions to transform to quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation. Irradiations were carried out both in situ and ex situ at room temperature and 1073 K up to 8 dpa. A thorough analysis of the microstructure shows no sign of radiation-induced dislocation loops, confirming that the observed black spots are indeed second-phase particles. After the first development of RHEAs in 2010, over 150 kinds of compositions have been reported, with their potential for use in high-temperature applications such as gas turbine engines and rocket nozzles. Various studies focused on ductility enhancement [,], better oxidation resistance [], and nuclear reactor material applications [,]. According to a review by Senkov et al. [], the only alloys to pass high-temperature compression tests at 1600°C were MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW. The main reason for the difficulty to perform compression tests at extremely high temperatures is the lack of suitable material as a jig material that provides high strength at extremely high temperatures. Recently, Wang et al. strengthened the grain boundary of an MoNbTaW-refractory high-entropy alloy through doping with B or C in trace amount, which simultaneously increases room-temperature strength and toughness []. This study provides a good strategy to increase the ductility of RHEAs by doping suitable elements.
